In English, a single personal pronoun th.why: A firm rule of English case, used constantly ('with him', 'for her', 'sit with me') and stated in every grammar of English; the subject forms after a preposition are rare errors. Bare pairs like 'with he' cannot be counted (the tokens also match 'with heavy', 'with health'), so it is counted on longer frames.

sources.note: Sampled hits are prefix matches ('sit with IHC', 'Ida', 'Ike'), not the subject form.

In English spelling, a sentence begins w.why: True and taught everywhere: the first word of a sentence is capitalized.

sources.quote: In all modern European languages, the first word in a sentence is capitalized, as is the first word in any quoted sentence.

The plural of the English noun 'woman' i.why: Deliberately false so the disjunction turns on the edited rule: the plural of 'woman' is 'women'.

sources.query: the plural of woman is women

After the preposition 'beside', the pron.why: A sentence this specific is not written anywhere, and nobody states the case form of 'he' after 'beside' on its own, yet people use 'he' for a man and say 'him' after prepositions every day.

sources.query: The auditor sat beside him all through the hearing
The auditor sat beside he all through the hearing

sources.note: The ordinary usage, the other premise.

After the preposition 'behind', the pron.why: Nobody states the case form of 'I' after 'behind' on its own, yet people say 'I' for themselves and use 'me' after prepositions all the time, so the form follows from those two facts.

sources.note: The ordinary usage, the other premise.

After the preposition 'to', the pronoun.why: This sentence is absent from the corpus, and nobody states the case form of 'she' after 'to' on its own; people do say 'she' for a woman and 'her' after prepositions constantly.

sources.query: The villagers waved goodbye to her
The villagers waved goodbye to she

sources.note: The ordinary usage, the other premise.

notes: TBox revision: a case rule (relation takes_case_form). Restricted to a single pronoun: coordinated ones ('between you and I') are a known hypercorrection and kept out of every prompt, as are 'than' and 'but', whose status as prepositions is disputed. Migrated to the new layout: the two indeterminate song-title queries ('Stand by me', 'Lean on me') and their worlds were removed (TBox has determinate queries only). Audit fixes: the cross-lingual questions (missed by two models, who answered 'she') and the paraphrase were fill-in-the-blank sentences; they now ask plainly which pronoun follows 'for' when it refers to a woman. Audit: the derived neopronoun queries (ze/hir, xe/xem) were missed by two models each (olmo and mistral on 'ze', olmo and llama on 'xe'), and these were genuine wrong choices, not format failures, since the models treat neopronouns as invariant. They are replaced by ordinary pronouns (he/him, I/me, she/her) with the object form stated in the prompt, so the rule is the only route; the third is an application (a children's-book editor). Not re-audited, since the models cannot be run from here. The propositional rule carries an example ('Sit with I'). Near unrelated asks the object of a verb ('us'), so a model that overgeneralises the edit to every object answers 'we' and is caught. Dl: a class inclusion with one filler.
